blocks.text: When a potential difference V is applied across the ends of a conductor, a current I starts flowing through it.

blocks.title: Ohm's law
blocks.text: The current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference applied across the conductor, provided there is no change in the physical state of the conductor. Mathematically V is proportional to I, or V = RI ... (9.31).
Here R is a constant known as the resistance of the conductor. The SI unit of resistance is the ohm, denoted by the Greek capital letter omega.

blocks.title: One ohm
blocks.text: The resistance of a conductor is 1 ohm if a current of 1 ampere flows through it when a potential difference of 1 volt is applied across its ends.

blocks.alt: Top left: electrons drifting left through a wire of length L and area A while the conventional current flows right, with I = nAvq. Top right: a straight V against I graph whose slope is R, and resistivity of copper rising in a straight line with temperature. Bottom left: Table 9.2 of resistivities and temperature coefficients. Bottom right: a cell of emf E with internal resistance r driving current through R, with a voltmeter, a switch and the power and emf formulae.
blocks.caption: Electric current, resistance and resistivity, power, emf and internal resistance (original diagram after Figures 9.20 to 9.26 and topics 9.10 to 9.15).
blocks.long_description: In a wire the free electrons drift slowly against the field, while the conventional current is taken in the opposite direction; the current equals the number of carriers per unit volume times the area, the drift speed and the charge. For a conductor in a fixed physical state the potential difference is proportional to the current, so the V against I graph is a straight line whose slope is the resistance. Resistance grows with length and falls with area, through the resistivity of the material, and for metals it rises steadily with temperature. A cell has an emf and an internal resistance: with the switch open a voltmeter reads the emf, and with a current flowing the terminal voltage falls by the current times the internal resistance.
